title: Melanoma researcher Georgina Long wins Prime Minister’s Prize for Science
content: Georgina Long and subatomic physicist Anthony Thomas recognised in Prime Minister’s Prizes for Science Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast When Prof Georgina Long was starting out in melanoma treatment and research, “my waiting room would change so rapidly”. Referring to her patients with stage 4 melanoma, the oncologist and medical director at the Melanoma Institute Australia said she wouldn’t “see the same face for more than nine months, 12 months maximum”.
summary: Oncologist Georgina Long, medical director of the Melanoma Institute Australia, was named a winner of the Prime Minister’s Prizes for Science. Her work has contributed to improved survival rates for patients with stage‑4 melanoma.
author: Guardian World

title: Nine Victorian datacentre projects await approval days before state election
content:
Days before the Victorian state election, nine datacentre projects are still pending approval, according to the ministerial permits register. Some companies say they expect to secure approval after Saturday, but the outcome remains uncertain. Among the projects is the West Footscray expansion of NextDC’s M3 datacentre, which Guardian Australia noted has encountered delays because of community opposition.

Political parties have released policies on permissible datacentre locations, though not all policies specify whether they apply retrospectively to existing proposals. The pending approvals therefore sit at the intersection of these policy positions and the upcoming election.
summary: Nine datacentre projects listed on the ministerial permits register remain awaiting approval just days before the Victorian state election. One of them, the West Footscray expansion of NextDC’s M3 datacentre, has faced delays due to community blowback.
author: Guardian World

title: Guardian poll shows Albanese's disapproval hits record as Australians reject AI datacentres
content:
The Guardian Essential poll reports that Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s disapproval rating has risen to its highest level, with his net popularity falling by ten points in a single month. The poll also shows a sharp decline in his overall approval ratings.

In a separate finding, the same survey indicates that nearly half of Australians oppose having an AI data centre near their home. The opposition is strongest among women, older respondents and supporters of One Nation and the Greens.
summary: Anthony Albanese’s net popularity fell 10 points in a month, putting his disapproval rating at its highest level in the Guardian Essential poll. The poll also found nearly half of Australians do not want an AI datacentre near their home, with women, older people and One Nation and Greens supporters most likely to oppose it.
author: Guardian World

title: Chinese police contact WeChat members discussing Melbourne vigil for HungryPanda rider
content:
Chinese police have reached out to several individuals who participated in a WeChat group created after the alleged murder of Feng Jianming, a HungryPanda food‑delivery rider. The group discussed attending a vigil in Melbourne for Feng, and at least three members reported that they or their parents received phone calls from police in their Chinese hometowns.

The contacts have prompted concerns that Chinese authorities may have become aware of the group’s discussion of protest activity, either through automatic monitoring or manual review of the Chinese‑owned messaging platform.
summary: Chinese police contact WeChat members discussing Melbourne vigil for HungryPanda rider.

title: Malaysia to deport thousands of migrants to Myanmar after ICJ genocide ruling
content: Malaysia announced it will repatriate thousands of migrants and refugees to Myanmar. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said the move will proceed even though the government recognizes that many of the asylum seekers have been victims of “atrocities” carried out by the junta in Naypyidaw. The decision was made days after the International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar had committed genocide against its Rohingya minority. Malaysia’s announcement follows the UN court’s finding of genocide against the Rohingya population.
summary: Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Malaysia will deport thousands of migrants and refugees to Myanmar, acknowledging many asylum seekers were victims of junta atrocities. The announcement came days after the ICJ ruled that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya minority.

title: Trump ignored intelligence on alleged Chinese spy tied to Nvidia co‑founder
content:
The source states that Donald Trump’s reaction to sensitive information that contradicts his worldview is presented as mirroring his conduct toward a potential war with Iran. It further claims that his unwillingness to heed warnings of suspected Chinese penetration of the tech company Nvidia follows a pattern of the U.S. president ignoring sensitive intelligence that conflicts with his perspective.  

According to the source, Trump disregarded repeated information that Nvidia co‑founder Jensen Huang was having an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy, a situation described as threatening Washington’s goal of surpassing China in the global artificial‑intelligence race.
summary: Trump has repeatedly ignored intelligence that contradicts his worldview, including warnings of suspected Chinese penetration of Nvidia. He also disregarded repeated information that Nvidia co‑founder Jensen Huang was having an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy, which threatened Washington’s goal of outpacing China in the artificial intelligence race.

title: Leaked data shows over 300 Russian troops killed while supporting Mali's junta
content:
Leaked records released exclusively show that 349 Russian personnel died in Mali over a three‑year period, a figure that exceeds three hundred. The documents also provide information about Russia’s military operations in other African countries.

One of the incidents detailed in the data is the assault on the northern town of Kidal on 25 April. According to a former member of Russia’s Africa Corps, who spoke anonymously, the attack began before dawn and caught the Russian fighters off guard. Within the first hour, insurgents overran checkpoints on the city’s outskirts and advanced toward the police station, where intense fighting broke out.

The witness described explosions and shouting throughout the engagement, noting that “nobody knew where the enemy was coming from.” The leaked data therefore links a high Russian casualty count to Moscow’s support for Mali’s junta and illustrates the volatility of Russian‑backed forces in the region.
summary: Leaked records list 349 Russian deaths in Mali over a three‑year period. The data describes a Russian‑backed attack on Kidal on 25 April, when insurgents overran outskirts checkpoints and fighting broke out at the police station.
author: Guardian World

title: NASA launches Discovery on classified STS‑33 mission for U.S. Military
content:
On November 22, 1989, the space shuttle Discovery lifted off from Kennedy Space Center on a secret U. S. Military mission, designated STS‑33. The launch occurred at night, making it the third nighttime launch in the shuttle program and the thirty‑second mission overall. Five astronauts aboard the orbiter were tasked with deploying a classified payload for the U. S. Department of Defense.

The payload believed to have been released by Discovery is thought to be a type of spy satellite known as Magnum. The specific mission of the satellite in orbit remains classified, and the details of its operations are not publicly disclosed.

The shuttle program was conceived as a compromise between civilian and military objectives. NASA intended the vehicle to support scientific research, enable on‑orbit servicing of commercial satellites, and assemble components for a space station. The Department of Defense viewed the shuttle as a platform for deploying and retrieving reconnaissance satellites and other classified projects. Following the loss of the Challenger, it was decided that the shuttle would be used for military missions only when they were essential to national security, while other needs would be met with expendable launch vehicles.

During the STS‑33 mission, the crew also celebrated Thanksgiving in space. The holiday began with a malfunction of the shuttle’s toilet, which the astronauts spent most of the day repairing before enjoying a turkey together.

For additional space‑history content, readers can explore the full “On This Day In Space” archive and view related videos on YouTube.
summary: On Nov. 22, 1989, the space shuttle Discovery launched on the secret mission STS-33 for the U.
author: Space.com

title: Oregon State University researchers grow potatoes in simulated lunar dust
content:
NASA is pursuing a permanent lunar presence, including plans for a moon base, which necessitates reliable food production systems for long-term human habitation. To address this challenge, researchers from the College of Agricultural Sciences at Oregon State University successfully grew potatoes in simulated lunar dust. The team published their findings on Nov. 20 in the Microgravity science journal, noting that potatoes completed their entire life cycle when the simulated soil was supplemented with organic matter.

The study utilized five different materials to simulate regolith, the dust and rocks covering the moon’s surface, representing both lunar mare and lunar highland regions. The researchers tested various concentrations of vermicompost, a nutrient-rich soil, mixed with the simulated regolith. They determined that a mixture containing 30 percent vermicompost yielded growth results comparable to those achieved in regular soil.

Aymeric Goyer, an associate professor at OSU’s Department of Botany and Plant Pathology, stated that this outcome is a significant step toward developing food production systems capable of supporting long-term lunar exploration. David Handy, a postdoctoral researcher in Goyer's lab, explained that the compost likely helps balance the toxicity of lunar regolith by reducing plant exposure to harmful compounds. The research suggests that future astronauts could bring nutrient-rich soil to mix with local regolith for farming, a strategy intended to avoid the high costs of shipping food from Earth. NASA provided funding for this research.
summary: Oregon State University scientists successfully grew potatoes in simulated lunar regolith mixed with 30 percent vermicompost. The study indicates that adding organic matter helps balance the toxicity of lunar soil, supporting future food production for moon exploration.
author: Space.com

title: Coogan and Brydon discuss literature, impersonations during Arctic Circle trip
content:
Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon have traveled to Scandinavia for a new installment of The Trip, which features a trip to the Arctic circle. The duo is currently staying at the Juvet Landskapshotell in Valldal, a location described as standing still amid mountains, pines, and yellowing birch in pale September light. During their stay, the actors take in the sights while engaging in discussions about various topics, including ageing, activism, and the northern lights.

Their conversations cover a wide range of subjects, from the playwrights August Strindberg and Henrik Ibsen to the persecuted genius of Galileo. Brydon notes that Ibsen fell in love with a teenager named Emilie when he was 60, prompting Coogan to comment that while he can imagine such a scenario, it does not mean he would do it. The dialogue also includes a brief exhortation on Palestine and a mention of the aurora borealis being spotted above Great Yarmouth. At one point, Brydon performs an extended impersonation of Melvyn Bragg presenting In Our Time, causing Coogan’s mouth to flicker.
summary: Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon ate breakfast at Juvet Landskapshotell in Scandinavia, where they discussed playwrights August Strindberg and Henrik Ibsen. They also talked about Galileo, Palestine, and the aurora borealis, and Brydon performed a Melvyn Bragg impersonation.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Donny Osmond recalls early fame, career collapse, and Michael Jackson
content: He was the child star of the Osmonds who become a global celebrity by 14. Then, at 21, his career came crashing down. Here, he reveals how he survived his years in exile – and what happened when Jackson was accused of child abuse For a brief period in the early 1970s, Donny Osmond ruled the world. He was the global teenage heart-throb. Even Michael Jackson trailed behind him. He was 14 when his most famous song, Puppy Love, spent five weeks at No 1 in the UK. My sister had a huge poster of him on her bedroom wall. Then again, everybody’s sister had a poster of him on their bedroom wall. Between 1972 and 1973 he had six Top 5 hits in the UK, three of them No 1s (including The Twelfth of Never and Young Love). He was equally successful back home in the US. Osmond was clean-cut, religious and respectful, with a mighty ability to punch out cover versions of saccharine standards. From his purple velvet cap to his doleful eyes and dazzling all-American smile, he was a marketing dream. We’d only just finished with Beatlemania. And now there was Donnymania.
summary: Donny Osmond became a global teen idol by age 14, topping UK charts with hits like "Puppy Love" and "The Twelfth of Never" during the early 1970s. His career collapsed at 21, and he later reflected on surviving exile and the impact of Michael Jackson's child‑abuse accusations.
author: Guardian Culture

title: 20 Long Books for Short Winter Days
content:
Light in the dark: 20 long books for short winter days invites readers to turn off their phones, get cosy, and commit to some of literature’s biggest and best novels. The piece highlights epic reads such as Don DeLillo’s Underworld and Eleanor Catton’s The Luminaries, encouraging readers to tackle projects that demand more time than the typical beach read.

The article notes that “Life starts all over again when it gets crisp in the fall,” a line from F Scott Fitzgerald’s The Great Gatsby, and suggests that the season is ideal for settling down to ambitious books. It contrasts slim works like Gatsby with larger‑scale titles that readers have been circling for some time, urging them to wrap themselves in a “bigger beast” as autumn turns to winter.

The author shares a personal anecdote about reading The Lord of the Rings at eight, which sparked a desire to write. That experience illustrates how long books can shape a reader’s imagination and keep them thinking about the story even while doing other things.
summary: The article lists 20 long novels, including Don DeLillo’s Underworld and Eleanor Catton’s The Luminaries, as ideal winter reads. It encourages readers to turn off their phones, get cozy, and commit to these epic books during the short winter days.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Netflix Documentary 'Primetime Preacher$' Exposes Televangelism Scandal
content: Netflix documentary Primetime Preacher$ travels back to a time when evangelism found a dominant place on US television – and the shocking tabloid stories that followed For three decades, film-maker Joe Berlinger has gripped true-crime buffs with his deep dives into small-town murders and infamous serial killers. His Netflix explorations of John Wayne Gacy and Jeffrey Dahmer helped flip documentary storytelling from viewer homework to a welcome distraction. After dedicating so much time to the life of Jeffrey Epstein, the kidnapping of JonBenét Ramsey and other unsolved mysteries, Berlinger thought Primetime Preacher$, his new Netflix documentary on America’s televangelist boom, would offer a break. But it turns out that’s a pretty juicy crime story too, about the religious right’s bank job on American politics. “The deeper resonance for me came when I realized that the global televangelism rise actually mirrors the rise of the religious right,” he says. “Religion and politics, from Reagan on, has really changed politics for the worse in my opinion. This was the birth of that.”
summary: Joe Berlinger directs 'Primetime Preacher$', a Netflix documentary that examines the rise of televangelism and the tabloid scandals that followed. Berlinger notes that the growth of televangelism mirrors the rise of the religious right and has negatively impacted American politics since Reagan.
author: Guardian Culture

title: New films portray Nazi collaborators sympathetically, including "Woman Unknown"
content: For decades, films about Nazi-occupied Europe were all about the fearless resistance while despicable collaborators deserved all they got. So what’s behind the spate of movies portraying turncoats in a more sympathetic light? A young maid busies herself in a vast, high-ceilinged apartment, serving her master steaming coffee in fine china and polishing the hefty family silver, as she picks her way across the checkerboard parquet lit by stylish Poul Henningsen lamps. Woman Unknown, which won the Golden Lion at the Venice film festival this year, is set in the immediate aftermath of Denmark’s liberation from Nazi rule, but you wouldn’t know that from the opening scenes: five years of occupation, martial law and rationing have left the splendour of the Danish bourgeoisie miraculously untouched. The trauma of wartime violence only comes rushing back in occasional bursts: blurry flashbacks show shadowy figures pointing guns at temples and bodies thudding to the floor. But the red fabric billowing through the fog of her memory is not the Nazi flag but liberated Denmark’s white-crossed Dannebrog. The black-clad executioners are not SS officers but resistance fighters reckoning with collaborators.
summary: For decades, films about Nazi-occupied Europe were all about the fearless resistance while despicable collaborators deserved all they got. So what’s behind the spate of movies portraying turncoats in a more sympathetic light?
author: Guardian Culture

title: Weird lifestyle advice from Gwyneth Paltrow: best podcasts of the week
content: The Hollywood star is joined by celebrity guests as she shares ‘practical tips’. Plus, David Cameron’s deeply personal series about Alzheimer’s The second podcast from her wellness empire is ostensibly centred on Paltrow’s incredibly niche lifestyle advice: where to eat the “best cacio e pepe in Rome”, for example, or “whether it’s weird to use an obsidian gua sha tool on a plane”. In reality, the show is a weekly cosy chat with a showbiz pal (first up, Zoe Saldaña) peppered with a few practical tips – such as how to eat enough protein if you can’t face any more eggs. Rachel Aroesti Widely available, episodes weekly
summary: Weird lifestyle advice from Gwyneth Paltrow: best podcasts of the week.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Documentary “You Can See Everything” tops $100 million global box office
content:
The documentary You Can See Everything, which follows fraudster Elizabeth Holmes in the weeks before her imprisonment, has crossed the $100 million mark at the global box office. The film, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, achieved the highest ever opening‑weekend figure for a non‑music documentary in the United Kingdom.

In North America, the film earned an estimated $2.5 million during its sixth week of release, according to Box Office Mojo. That weekend revenue brought the North American total to $93.5 million. Additional releases in several international territories added an estimated $9 million, raising the worldwide total to $102.5 million.
summary: Documentary “You Can See Everything” tops $100 million global box office.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Tennis Australia supports Taylah Lessue after online death threats in Adelaide
content: Taylah Lessue had been suffering from glandular fever before loss Police investigating death threats sent to 18-year-old Tennis Australia has thrown its support behind up-and-coming player Taylah Lessue after a slew of “abhorrent” online abuse and death threats were directed at the 18-year-old at a tournament in Adelaide. Lessue appeared at the City of Playford Tennis International on Sunday, winning the first set of a qualifying match against Ashleigh Simes 6-4 before dropping the next two to love as fatigue, chest tightness and muscle spasms set in.
summary: Tennis Australia has expressed support for 18-year-old Taylah Lessue following online abuse and death threats received during a tournament in Adelaide. Lessue lost a qualifying match against Ashleigh Simes while suffering from glandular fever and physical symptoms.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Lights Out Delays Game as Commanders Win 22-20 Over Bengals on Field Goal
content:
The Washington Commanders defeated the Cincinnati Bengals 22-20 on Monday night, securing a victory with a final-second field goal. The game featured a third-quarter delay caused by a power outage, but the decisive plays occurred late in the fourth quarter. With 39 seconds remaining and no timeouts, the Commanders took possession after the Bengals had taken a 20-19 lead on a 56-yard field goal by Evan McPherson.

Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels orchestrated the final drive, connecting with rookie Antonio Williams on two long passes that advanced the team 64 yards in 34 seconds. Daniels first hit Williams for 22 yards and then found him again for a 42-yard catch-and-run, placing the ball in the Cincinnati eight-yard line. After Daniels spiked the ball with five seconds left, kicker Drew Stevens successfully converted a 26-yard field goal as time expired to complete the upset.
summary: Lights Out Delays Game as Commanders Win 22-20 Over Bengals on Field Goal.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Steve Smith falls cheaply on return in NSW vs Queensland Sheffield Shield match
content:
Steve Smith made a laborious 12 for NSW against Queensland in a Sheffield Shield match, ending his batting comeback with a cheap dismissal. The veteran batsman had not played an innings since 22 October, when he suffered a neck injury during Australia’s second Test in South Africa. His return for NSW comes ahead of Australia’s first Test against New Zealand, which begins on 9 December in Perth.

Meanwhile, opener Sam Konstas strengthened his claims for Test recall by scoring 42 off 86 balls. Smith’s recent Sheffield Shield appearance was cut short by Michael Neser, marking a difficult start to his return to the domestic circuit.
summary: Steve Smith made a laborious 12 for NSW against Queensland in their Sheffield Shield clash. He had not played an innings since 22 October, when he battled a neck injury in Australia’s second Test in South Africa.
author: Guardian Sport

title: ‘Ollie makes it sound easy’: Crocombe on fast-track with Test debut in his sights
content: England seamer, who now has Jimmy Anderson as a county teammate, hopes a red-ball bow is not too far away Henry Crocombe is a cricketer in a hurry. Thoughts of playing for England were far from the fast bowler’s mind at the start of 2026, but he has since appeared in all three squads, made his debut in two formats and swapped Sussex for Surrey. The winter move to the Oval has come in part due to the financial problems at Hove. But the chance to play and train at a Test ground made it a no-brainer when Alec Stewart sat him down at the Fentiman Arms in SW8 with a contract offer. The subsequent signing of Jimmy Anderson was simply an added bonus.
summary: ‘Ollie makes it sound easy’: Crocombe on fast-track with Test debut in his sights.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Javokhir Sindarov: 20-year-old Uzbek grandmaster can't play games just for fun
content: In an exclusive interview with the Guardian ahead of the most important match of his life, the Uzbek prodigy talks Messi, GTA VI and the competitive streak he can’t switch off Read our World Chess Championship watch guide Javokhir Sindarov has a problem. The fast-rising 20-year-old Uzbek grandmaster, who is challenging for the world chess championship over the next three weeks in Switzerland, can’t stop playing for keeps. Even when he is off the clock and meant to be relaxing with friends, a compulsion to win takes hold. His preferred escape is Counter-Strike, the tactical first-person shooter that has become one of the world’s most popular esports. But he also plays EA Sports FC ( née Fifa ), the all-conquering soccer kickabout, and approaches both with the same seriousness of purpose that has propelled him toward the pinnacle of his day job. “I’m the guy who can’t play games just for fun,” Sindarov tells the Guardian less than 48 hours before Tuesday’s world championship opener in Geneva, smiling at the absurdity of it. “If I play something, I always try to learn, trying to become better.”
summary: Uzbek grandmaster Javokhir Sindarov is challenging for the world chess championship in Switzerland but struggles to relax due to a compulsion to win. He approaches video games like Counter-Strike and EA Sports FC with the same serious intent as his chess career.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Grand Theft Auto VI use by NBA and NFL stars raises concerns over performance
content:
ESPN pundit Stephen A Smith recently criticized NBA and NFL stars for their intense focus on Grand Theft Auto VI, questioning how players can maintain professional dedication while allegedly addicted to the game. Smith’s comments highlighted a broader debate regarding whether late-night gaming negatively impacts elite athletes’ performance. This scrutiny extended to football, where Manchester United fans questioned Bryan Mbeumo’s professionalism after he shared a GTA VI image with the caption “ historique” late Thursday night.

The concern over gaming distractions also influenced pre-match predictions for the Premier League. The Odd Sport social media account forecast that Chelsea, Brighton, and Manchester City would lose their upcoming games, arguing that their younger squads might prioritize Vice City over their opponents. This prediction suggested that such distractions could lead to reduced intensity on the pitch. By Monday, this specific forecast had garnered tens of thousands of likes, reflecting significant public interest in the potential link between video game engagement and athletic focus.
summary: ESPN’s Stephen A Smith criticized NBA and NFL stars for playing Grand Theft Auto VI, saying it could harm their performance. An Odd Sport social media account predicted that Chelsea, Brighton and Manchester City would lose before last weekend’s Premier League games because their younger squads might be more focused on the game.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya's shoulder injury not too serious, no surgery needed
content:
Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta stated that goalkeeper David Raya’s shoulder injury is “not too serious” and does not require surgery. Raya was forced off in the second half of Saturday’s 2-2 draw with Newcastle due to a suspected dislocated shoulder. Although he missed training on Monday following an MRI scan, Arteta expressed hope that the injury is better than initially feared.

Raya will miss Tuesday’s Champions League match against Borussia Dortmund, with Kepa Arrizabalaga expected to start in his place. Arteta indicated that Raya could potentially return for a subsequent clash against Manchester City.
summary: Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya will miss the Champions League match against Borussia Dortmund due to a suspected dislocated shoulder. Manager Mikel Arteta said the injury is not too serious and no surgery is required.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Marco Penge wins RSM Classic in Georgia, earns 2027 PGA Tour card
content: England’s Marco Penge won the RSM Classic in Georgia after birdieing the first extra hole of a four‑man playoff. The victory gave him his first PGA Tour title and secured his card for the 2027 season.
summary: England's Marco Penge birdied the first extra hole in a four‑man play‑off to win the RSM Classic in Georgia. The victory secured him a PGA Tour card for 2027.
author: BBC Sport

title: Arsenal and PSG eye RB Leipzig winger Antonio Nusa
content: Arsenal and Paris Saint‑Germain are reportedly interested in RB Leipzig winger Antonio Nusa. Xabi Alonso has the backing of Chelsea’s hierarchy for a potential move. Meanwhile, Liverpool has opened contract talks with goalkeeper Alisson Becker, with additional developments to follow.
summary: Arsenal and PSG are both looking at a move for RB Leipzig winger Antonio Nusa. Xabi Alonso has Chelsea hierarchy backing, and Liverpool has opened contract talks with keeper Alisson Becker.

title: Tarkowski's first Premier League red ruins Moyes' night - was it deserved?
content: Everton captain James Tarkowski received his first Premier League red card in Monday’s 4‑0 defeat to Brentford. The decision has sparked debate over whether it was harsh.
summary: Everton captain James Tarkowski was sent off for the first time in his Premier League career in Monday's 4-0 loss at Brentford - but was it a harsh decision?
author: BBC Sport

title: Iowa lead detonation plan stalled as appeals court declines to intervene
content: Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand (D) referred the decision on the Army’s plan to detonate tons of explosive lead material in Iowa to President Trump on Monday, as a federal appeals court declined to intervene. Earlier that day, Trump stated he personally supported detonating the lead-containing munitions.
summary: The Army's plan to detonate explosive lead material in Iowa is on hold after Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand (D) sent the decision back to President Trump. A federal appeals court declined to intervene, while Trump said he personally supports the detonation.
author: The Hill

title: Trump, Iowa Gov‑elect Rob Sand Reject Army's Lead Munitions Detonation
content: President Trump and Iowa Gov‑elect Rob Sand (D) have both indicated they do not wish to take responsibility for a political controversy surrounding the Army’s planned detonation of lead‑containing munitions in Iowa. The Army had been set to proceed with the test on Wednesday, but Trump announced on Monday that he would not move forward with the operation.
summary: President Trump and Iowa Gov‑elect Rob Sand (D) have said they will not support the Army's planned detonation of lead‑containing munitions in Iowa, which has sparked public outcry. The Army had been ready to proceed with the detonation on Wednesday, but Trump announced on Monday that he would not move forward with the plan.
author: The Hill

title: Pennsylvania reports ninth measles death of unvaccinated Centre County resident
content:
Pennsylvania health officials confirmed the state’s ninth measles‑related death this year on Monday, occurring less than a week after the U.S. lost its measles elimination status after more than 25 years.

The Pennsylvania Department of Health reported that an unvaccinated resident of Centre County died after testing positive for the virus. The state has recorded 1,638 measles cases.
summary: Pennsylvania health officials confirmed the state's ninth measles-related death this year. The death involved an unvaccinated Centre County resident who tested positive for the virus, and the state has recorded 1,638 measles cases.
author: The Hill

title: Trump, Iowa Gov.-elect, Halts Army Lead Detonation Plan
content: The Army’s proposal to detonate tons of explosive lead material in Iowa has stalled. The plan was put on hold after Iowa Gov‑elect Rob Sand (D) passed a decision on Monday, leaving the project in limbo.
summary: Trump and Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand (D) are involved in the decision over the Army's plan to detonate tons of explosive lead material in Iowa. The plan is now in limbo after the decision was passed.
author: The Hill

title: Federal court unseals heavily redacted documents on raid of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s D.C. home
content: A federal court released unsealed, heavily redacted records on Monday that pertain to the search of Representative Ilhan Omar’s Washington, D.C., home last month. Federal prosecutors had made a last‑minute attempt to block the release of the files. The documents disclose limited information about the scope of the investigation, indicating that federal investigators sought evidence.
summary: A federal court on Monday released unsealed records related to the search of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s (D-Minn.) Washington, D.
author: The Hill

title: White House requests billions in stopgap funding for federal agencies
content: The White House sent Congress a 12-page “anomalies” request on Monday, asking for billions of dollars in additional funding to be included in a stopgap spending bill. The document outlines exceptions to current spending levels for federal agencies, which lawmakers are expected to take up next month.
summary: The White House is asking Congress to include billions of dollars in additional funding in a stopgap spending bill to fund federal agencies. The 12-page anomalies request, sent Monday, outlines exceptions to current spending levels that would allow the Trump administration to keep agencies funded.
author: The Hill

title: Army seeks federal approval to resume helicopter training near Reagan National Airport
content:
The U.S. Army has requested federal approval to resume helicopter training flights near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport. The request follows a deadly midair collision over the Potomac River that killed 67 people nearly two years ago.  

Representative Don Beyer (D‑Va.) said Monday that Army officials had briefed his office on the proposal.
summary: The Army is seeking federal approval to resume helicopter training flights near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, drawing safety concerns nearly two years after a deadly midair collision over the Potomac River killed 67 people. Rep.
author: The Hill

title: Army to detonate lead-containing munitions in Iowa on Wednesday
content: The U.S. Army will detonate lead‑containing munitions in Iowa on Wednesday, following President Trump’s added uncertainty on Monday. Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said the controlled removal will proceed in full coordination with state, local and federal authorities, prioritizing the safety of Iowa’s citizens.
summary: The Army will detonate lead-containing munitions in Iowa on Wednesday. Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said the removal will be coordinated with state, local and federal authorities to protect Iowa’s citizens.
author: The Hill

title: California Democrat Rep. Gomez resigns following ethics report on sexual misconduct allegations
content: California Democrat Congressman Rep. Jimmy Gomez announced he will resign after a House Ethics report found his conduct violated House rules by “making unwelcome sexual advances.” The report concluded that Gomez’s actions breached the established standards of conduct for members of Congress.
summary: California Democrat Rep. Gomez resigns following ethics report on sexual misconduct allegations.
author: NPR Politics

title: Robert Macfarlane calls trust in COP climate summits misplaced
content:
Robert Macfarlane, a nature writer, delivered his first Reith lecture in which he criticized the effectiveness of the COP climate summits. He said that “misplacing our trust” in the COP process undermines the ability to achieve consequential climate change action.  

Macfarlane’s remarks were recorded before the 31st UN climate summit failed to produce an agreement on actions to combat global heating.  

He expressed “much more hope” in emerging alliances such as the Santa Marta process, a smaller group of countries that have pledged to phase out fossil fuels as soon as possible.
summary: Robert Macfarlane calls trust in COP climate summits misplaced.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Music therapy before and during coronary angiography linked to lower systolic blood pressure
content: A comparative clinical trial published online in the journal Heart found that music therapy administered before and during coronary angiography—an invasive test that visualizes blood flow in the coronary arteries—was linked to lower systolic blood pressure, the higher number in a blood‑pressure reading.
summary: A comparative clinical trial found that music therapy before and during coronary angiography was associated with lower systolic blood pressure. The study was published online in the journal Heart.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Teenage salty snack consumption raises adult IBD risk
content: A large long‑term study published online in the journal Gut found that a high intake of salty snacks during the teenage years is linked to a heightened risk of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)—including Crohn’s disease, ulcerative colitis, or a mix of both—in young adulthood. The study highlights the potential long‑term health impact of adolescent snacking habits.
summary: A large long‑term study published online in the journal Gut found that high intake of salty snacks during the teenage years is linked to a heightened risk of inflammatory bowel disease in young adulthood. The study covers Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, or a mix of both.
author: Medical Xpress

title: High-velocity pickleball eye hit may increase glaucoma risk, doctors warn
content: Doctors warn that being struck in the eye by a high‑velocity pickleball can increase the risk of glaucoma. The warning appeared in the online journal BMJ Case Reports after the authors treated a female player who sustained such an injury.
summary: Doctors warn that a high-velocity pickleball can increase glaucoma risk after treating a female player. The warning was published in the online journal BMJ Case Reports.
author: Medical Xpress

title: ICE operation in Minneapolis likely led to fewer health care visits for Spanish-speaking patients, analysis finds
content: A recent analysis suggests that the ICE operation in Minneapolis reduced health‑care visits among Spanish‑speaking patients. From December 2025 through February 2026, roughly 2,000 ICE agents operated in the Minneapolis‑Saint Paul metro area, heightening raids, arrests and violence as part of Operation Metro Surge.
summary: ICE operation in Minneapolis likely led to fewer health care visits for Spanish-speaking patients, analysis finds.
author: Medical Xpress

title: New LSU Review Shows Gestational Diabetes Carries Long-Term Health Risks
content: A recent review from LSU’s Pennington Biomedical Research Center challenges the common view that gestational diabetes ends with childbirth. The study shows that the condition’s health effects can persist for years, raising cardiometabolic risks for mothers. It also suggests that these long‑term risks may influence the future health of their children.
summary: Gestational diabetes is often viewed as a complication of pregnancy that resolves after delivery. A new review led by researchers from LSU's Pennington Biomedical Research Center shows that its health implications can extend for years, increasing cardiometabolic risks for mothers and potentially affecting the future health of their children.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Alzheimer's drug diranersen shows clinical benefit in CELIA trial interim results
content: Interim results of the CELIA trial—testing the Alzheimer’s drug diranersen—were presented this week at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer’s Disease (CTAD 2026) conference in Boston, U.S. Professor Cath Mummery of UCL Queen Square Institute of Neurology and UCLH is one of the study’s principal investigators.
summary: Interim results from the first two years of the CELIA trial of diranersen were presented at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer's Disease (CTAD 2026) conference in Boston. Professor Cath Mummery of UCL Queen Square Institute of Neurology and UCLH is a principal investigator of the study.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Wolbachia Mosquito Intervention Cuts Arboviral Infections 68.6% in Brazilian Children
content: Researchers report that a Wolbachia‑based mosquito intervention, designed to curb dengue, Zika and chikungunya, substantially reduces arboviral infections among school‑aged children in Brazil. The EVITA dengue trial in Belo Horizonte found 68.6 % efficacy in reducing arboviral infections among participating children.
summary: A Wolbachia-based (wMel) mosquito intervention reduced arboviral infections among school‑aged children in Brazil. The EVITA dengue trial in Belo Horizonte found 68.6% efficacy in reducing arboviral infections.
author: Medical Xpress

title: University of Glasgow spinoff develops handheld ozone device for hospital sink drains
content: A University of Glasgow spinoff has developed a handheld device that uses ozone generated from fresh air to tackle contaminated sink drains, a persistent and overlooked source of hospital infections.
summary: A University of Glasgow spinoff has developed a handheld device that generates ozone from fresh air. The device is intended to address contaminated sink drains, a persistent and overlooked source of hospital infection.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Local measurements reveal global quantum properties in a constant number of experimental runs
content: Verifying quantum devices becomes increasingly difficult as the number of qubits grows, because describing a general quantum state requires an exponential number of parameters. Consequently, full state tomography becomes impractical for larger systems. However, most experiments do not require a complete state description; instead, they focus on specific properties such as whether the state is close to the target, if qubits are entangled, or if the system possesses resources necessary for quantum computation.
summary: A quantum device with more qubits is harder to verify. Describing a general quantum state takes an exponential number of parameters, and reconstructing it in full—a procedure known as state tomography—becomes impractical as the system grows.
author: Phys.org

title: Researchers uncover recipe for Taxol, suggesting tobacco plants could produce the drug
content: Researchers are working to decode the natural production process of Taxol (paclitaxel), a widely used cancer drug. Their goal is to make the drug’s production cheaper and more efficient. This effort responds to the expected global increase in cancer diagnoses.
summary: Researchers are working to understand how the cancer drug Taxol (paclitaxel) is naturally produced, as the trend of cancer diagnoses is expected to continue. The goal is to make its production cheaper and more efficient.
author: Phys.org

title: Genetic mosaic explains diverse beak forms in Darwin's finches
content:
Genetic mosaic helps explain diverse forms of Darwin's finches. The birds are known for their varied beaks, which allow them to take advantage of different food sources in the Galápagos Islands.

Much previous research has focused on seed‑eating ground finches, but their relatives that search for insects in forested areas have received less attention.
summary: Darwin's finches have varied beaks that help them exploit different food sources in the Galápagos Islands. Most research has focused on seed‑eating ground finches, while insect‑hunting relatives in forested areas have received less attention.
author: Phys.org

title: CNRS Study Finds Violin Tone Improves Without Physical Change
content:
A study published in Acta Acustica challenges the common belief that a violin’s sound improves with regular playing. Led by a CNRS researcher, the experiment involved a professional soloist who played the instrument for six months. The musician reported that the violin had become easier to play and its tone had improved, judging the process complete by the end of the period.

Despite the player’s positive assessment, the study found no physical or acoustic measurement confirming that the instrument underwent a mechanical change. The results suggest that the perceived improvement in the violin’s characteristics did not result from actual physical alterations to the instrument itself.
summary: A CNRS-led experiment published in Acta Acustica found that a violin's improved tone after six months of playing was not supported by any physical or acoustic measurements. The professional soloist reported the instrument became easier to play and its tone improved, but the study showed no mechanical change in the instrument.
author: Phys.org

title: OpenAI and Anthropic AI models solve hundreds of long‑standing math problems
content: In 2026, mathematics faced an identity crisis as frontier AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic made stunning progress on hundreds of open problems that had baffled mathematicians for decades—and centuries in some cases. These breakthroughs are said to have forever changed the field.
summary: In 2026, AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic made stunning progress on hundreds of open mathematical problems. The field of mathematics was said to have an identity crisis and was forever changed.
author: Phys.org

title: Temporary Disability: A Right for All Workers Under Social Security
content:
In discussions of workplace absenteeism, temporary disability is highlighted as a right rather than an expense. The policy is positioned as a fundamental element of the public Social Security system.

It is a right for all workers who fall ill and a social security benefit designed primarily to protect those who are sick. The benefit enables workers to receive medical treatment, recover or improve their condition, and ensures they have sufficient income during periods in which they are unable to work.
summary: Temporary disability is a cornerstone of the public Social Security system. It is a right for all workers who fall ill, providing them with income while they receive medical treatment and recover.
author: Phys.org

title: Scotland's Food & Drink SMEs Risk Losing Funding to Cut Emissions, Heriot-Watt Finds
content: Research from Heriot‑Watt University finds that Scotland’s small food and drink businesses face significant financial and operational barriers that could prevent them from accessing vital funding to reduce emissions from keeping produce cold. The study highlights the risk that these SMEs may be frozen out of necessary support to tackle energy challenges.
summary: Scotland's small food and drink businesses face significant financial and operational barriers that could prevent them from accessing vital funding to reduce emissions from keeping produce cold. The research was conducted by Heriot-Watt University.
author: Phys.org

title: AML May Begin Over 50 Years Before Diagnosis, Study Finds
content:
A new study shows acute myeloid leukemia can begin more than 50 years before diagnosis. In two‑thirds of cases, the first cancer‑driving mutation appears before age 20.

Researchers found that the mutated cells grow in predictable patterns, accelerating dramatically as additional mutations accumulate.
summary: A study shows acute myeloid leukemia can start developing more than 50 years before diagnosis. The first cancer‑driving mutation appears before age 20 in two‑thirds of cases, and mutated cells grow in surprisingly predictable patterns that accelerate dramatically as additional mutations accumulate.
author: Science Daily

title: Lower Spinal Bone Density Linked to Faster Brain Aging, Study Finds
content:
New research links lower spinal bone density to faster cognitive decline and accelerated changes in the brain’s white matter.  
The connection suggests routine medical scans could uncover hidden warning signs of brain aging and identify people at increased risk of dementia.
summary: New research links lower spinal bone density to faster cognitive decline and accelerated changes in the brain's white matter. Routine medical scans could uncover hidden warning signs of brain aging and identify people at increased risk of dementia.
author: Science Daily

title: A Power Provider for Meta Urged Regulators to Exempt Data Center Plants From Acid Rain Rules
content: The EPA met with industry players before recommending a waiver of acid‑rain regulations for certain data‑center power plants. Among those players was Williams, a gas power provider that supplies electricity to Meta data centers.
summary: Before the EPA recommended waiving acid rain regulations for certain data-center power plants, it met with industry players—including Williams, a gas power provider for Meta data centers.
author: Wired

title: Google Undid Product Manager's Efforts to Map Israeli Checkpoints for Palestinians
content: A Google product manager had set out to accurately map Israeli checkpoints in the West Bank on Google Maps. However, the company later reversed that effort, undoing the work he had completed.
summary: A product manager at Google worked to accurately map Israeli checkpoints in the West Bank on Google Maps. The company later reversed his work, undoing the mapping.
author: Wired

title: Oregon, Virginia AGs Sue Elon Musk Companies Over Weak Deepfake Safeguards
content: The attorneys general of Oregon and Virginia have filed a lawsuit against SpaceX and other Elon Musk‑owned companies, alleging that the firms have weak safeguards against sexualized imagery of real individuals, including children, in connection with the Grok deep‑fake technology.
summary: The attorneys general of Oregon and Virginia have filed a lawsuit against several of Elon Musk’s companies. The suit alleges the companies have weak safeguards against sexualized imagery of real people, including children.
author: Wired

title: Nvidia employees split over Jensen Huang's return
content: Some saw Huang’s resignation as an opportunity for culture change at the chip giant. “If Jensen comes back, I’m not doing any HR trainings ever again,” one employee said.
summary: Some staff saw Huang’s resignation as an opportunity for culture change at the chip giant. One employee said they would not do any HR trainings if Jensen returns.
author: Wired

content: Too big to fail, the sequel. | Image: The Verge; Getty Images I suppose I must issue a hearty congratulations to Jensen Huang. Huang is CEO of Nvidia again, to the surprise of basically everyone except President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, who made sure it happened. Now, those of us who had some kind of basic education on what a "free market" is might find it objectionable to have the American president strong-arming a major American company. But our billionaire tech overlords care about the "free market" exactly as much as they care about "free speech," which is to say not at all. Watching Silicon Valley cheer for what is, effectively, a sign of a command economy has certainly been brac …

title: Trump backs Jensen Huang’s return after Nvidia board accepts his resignation
content: After Nvidia's board accepted Jensen Huang's resignation as CEO, following reports that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, President Donald Trump, too, appeared to submit to the new reality. Appearing on Stephen A. Smith's radio show shortly after the news came out, Trump said that Huang would "end up on his feet." "You know the expression, anybody can be replaced," Trump said, floating Apple's ex-CEO Tim Cook as a potential CEO candidate. It didn't take long for Trump to begin softening his approach, making it clear he'd welcome Huang back into the role of CEO even if Nvidia's own board wasn't ready to do so. Behind the scen …
